meaning: Used in place of “we” or even “me”. It holds the speaker and Jah, and the speaker and every other person, together as one. No one is reduced to “you” or “me”.
usage: “I and I a go a di Issembly tomorrow.”

meaning: Natural, pure and full of life. Most often used of food, but it can describe anything that feeds the life force.
The Rastafari way of life as a whole: diet, speech, dress, prayer and how you treat others. Many prefer it to the word “religion”.
usage: “It's not a religion, it's a livity.”

meaning: Why stand under something you have grasped? To overstand is to rise above a thing by knowing it fully.
“Op” sounds like “up”, but oppression pushes people down. So the word is made to say what it does.
usage: “Downpressor man, where you gonna run to?”

meaning: Unity, with the “I” placed first: oneness that begins with each person's own divinity.
Creation, all that Jah made. Many words take the I-sound to bring them closer to the divine.
Praises, especially chanted praises to Jah during a Nyabinghi Issembly.
usage: “Send up Ises to the Most High.”

meaning: Politics as trickery: the games Babylon plays with poor people's lives.
usage: “Dem ah play politricks wid di people.”

meaning: The corrupt, oppressive system of the West and its institutions, especially the police. Taken from the city of captivity in scripture.
The promised land. For most Rastas this is Africa, and Ethiopia in particular.
Good, pleasing, at peace. Often used as a greeting.
Someone without locks, or more broadly someone who lives by Babylon's ways.
usage: “Him a bald-head, but him have a good heart.”

meaning: A blessing and a farewell: an aspiration to rise spiritually.
Rastas say “Selassie I” with the letter I, not “the First”, so the name also holds the divine “I”.
usage: “Give thanks and praises to Selassie I.”
